bio.en: Founder of Wahhabism, whose 1744 pact with Emir Muhammad bin Saud laid the foundation of the first Saudi state.
One of Europe's first women scientists. Translated and annotated Newton's Principia into French and wrote on fire and energy; Voltaire's companion.
Founding Father and signer of the Declaration of Independence who studied electricity and invented the lightning rod and bifocals.
Created the unified classification of living things and the two-part naming of species that biologists still use.
One of the greatest mathematicians, with over 800 works. Spent most of his career at the St Petersburg Academy, working on even after going blind.

role.en: husband of Maria Theresa and founder of the Habsburg-Lorraine dynasty

bio.en: A duke of Lorraine who swapped Lorraine for Tuscany and married Maria Theresa. Elected emperor in 1745, he left government to his wife, ran the court's finances shrewdly and built the collection that became the core of Vienna's Natural History Museum.

role.en: child shogun who died at the age of seven

bio.en: Ienobu's son, made shogun in 1713 at the age of three while Arai Hakuseki and Manabe Akifusa governed. His death in 1716 ended Ieyasu's direct line, and the shogunate passed to Yoshimune of the Kii branch.
Daughter of Peter the Great who came to power in the guards' coup of 1741. She founded Moscow University and the Academy of Arts, and in the Seven Years' War her army occupied Berlin.

role.en: king under whom France lost Canada

bio.en: He became king at five and reigned for almost 59 years. In the Seven Years’ War France lost Canada and most of its Indian possessions to Britain, while his mistresses Madame de Pompadour and du Barry embodied court extravagance.
Fisherman's son who became Russia's first native academician: chemist, physicist, poet and language reformer who inspired Moscow University.
Presided over the Qing Empire at its largest and richest; a lavish patron of the arts who rebuffed Britain's Macartney embassy.
Empiricist sceptic: we never observe causation but infer it from habit, and morality is rooted in feeling rather than reason. Kant said Hume woke him from his "dogmatic slumber".
Made Prussia a great power and survived the Seven Years' War against Austria, Russia and France. An 'enlightened despot' and friend of Voltaire.
Genevan Enlightenment thinker whose The Social Contract and idea of popular sovereignty inspired the French Revolution.

role.en: ailing shogun whose speech only one courtier understood

bio.en: Yoshimune's son, shogun 1745–1760. He had a severe speech impediment, and his orders were relayed by Ōoka Tadamitsu; real power lay with his father and then with his councillors.
Author of Dream of the Red Chamber, one of China's Four Great Classical Novels and the summit of its prose fiction.

role.en: boy emperor who moved the court back to Moscow

bio.en: Grandson of Peter the Great, he took the throne at eleven. He toppled Menshikov and moved the court to Moscow, where the Dolgorukov princes held sway; he died of smallpox at fourteen, ending the male Romanov line.
Only woman to head the Habsburg lands. Defended her inheritance in the War of the Austrian Succession, reformed schools and army; mother of Marie Antoinette.

role.en: sultan who lost the war to Catherine II

bio.en: He started the Russo-Turkish war of 1768–1774, in which his fleet was burned at Chesma and his army routed at Kagul. He tried to reform the army and founded a naval engineering school, dying before peace was made.

Taught that happiness lies in knowing oneself and in "congenial work" suited to one's nature. He spent his last 25 years as a wanderer; his epitaph reads "The world tried to catch me, but did not succeed".
Founder of modern economics whose The Wealth of Nations described the division of labour and the 'invisible hand' of the market.
Founder of German classical philosophy, author of the Critique of Pure Reason and the categorical imperative. Rarely left Königsberg.
A navigator-priest from Raiatea who sailed with Cook, drew a chart of 74 Pacific islands and interpreted for the Māori.

role.en: sultan of the Küçük Kaynarca peace and the loss of Crimea

bio.en: Right after his accession he signed the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca (1774), recognising Crimean independence; Russia annexed the peninsula in 1783. He died in the midst of a new war with Russia and Austria.
Made three Pacific voyages, charting New Zealand and Australia's east coast and reaching Hawaii, where he was killed.

role.en: emperor who freed the nobility from compulsory service

bio.en: Grandson of Peter the Great, raised in Holstein. In six months he issued the Manifesto on the Freedom of the Nobility and made peace with Prussia; he was overthrown in a coup by his wife Catherine and soon killed at Ropsha.
Ruled Russia for 34 years, annexing Crimea and New Russia, joining the partitions of Poland and corresponding with Voltaire.
Never lost a battle. Stormed the fortress of Izmail, led the Italian and Swiss campaigns of 1799 and wrote The Science of Victory.
Greatest artist of Brazilian Baroque who, crippled by disease, worked with tools strapped to his hands, carving the prophets of Congonhas.

role.en: first President of the United States

bio.en: Commander of the Continental Army in the War of Independence and first US President; the nation's capital bears his name.

role.en: 2nd US president, one of the Founding Fathers

bio.en: A Massachusetts lawyer and the first US vice president. As president he kept the country out of a full war with France but signed the unpopular Alien and Sedition Acts; he was the first to live in the White House (1800).
Perfected the steam engine that powered the Industrial Revolution. The unit of power, the watt, is named after him.

role.en: shogun of the Tanuma era and the Tenmei famine

bio.en: Shogun 1760–1786, he left government to Tanuma Okitsugu, who promoted commerce and monopolies and became notorious for bribery. His last years were darkened by the eruption of Mount Asama (1783) and the Great Tenmei Famine.
Inca descendant who led the largest indigenous revolt against Spanish rule in Peru; brutally executed in Cusco.

role.en: first Governor of New South Wales

bio.en: Commanded the convict First Fleet and in 1788 founded Sydney, the first British settlement in Australia.

role.en: king under whom Britain lost its American colonies

bio.en: Reigned for 60 years. Under him Britain lost its 13 American colonies but defeated Napoleon, and in 1801 united with Ireland to form the United Kingdom. He suffered severe mental illness, and from 1811 a regent ruled in his place.

role.en: infant emperor who spent his whole life imprisoned

bio.en: Proclaimed emperor at two months old and deposed by Elizabeth a year later. He spent his life in prison and was killed by his guards in Shlisselburg Fortress when Mirovich tried to free him.

Son of Maria Theresa, who after her death in 1780 unleashed a torrent of reforms: the Patent of Toleration (1781), the end of personal serfdom and the closure of hundreds of monasteries. Resistance was so fierce that he revoked much of it himself before he died.
Posing as Emperor Peter III, he led Russia's largest Cossack and peasant uprising (1773–1775) before being executed in Moscow.

role.en: third President of the United States

bio.en: Principal author of the Declaration of Independence who, as president, doubled the country with the Louisiana Purchase.
Former slave who led the revolt in Saint-Domingue, abolished slavery and paved the way for Haitian independence; died in a French prison.
Suvorov's pupil and commander-in-chief in 1812 who fought Napoleon at Borodino and drove the Grande Armée out of Russia.
Spanish court painter who exposed cruelty in Los Caprichos, The Disasters of War, The Third of May 1808 and the haunting Black Paintings.

role.en: Tuscan reformer who was first in Europe to abolish the death penalty

bio.en: He ruled Tuscany for twenty-five years and in 1786 became the first in Europe to abolish the death penalty and torture there. As emperor he calmed Hungary and the Netherlands, which had revolted under Joseph II, and signed the Declaration of Pillnitz with Prussia against revolutionary France.

Founder of utilitarianism: the right action brings the greatest happiness to the greatest number. He argued for abolishing slavery and the death penalty; his preserved body is still kept at University College London.
Germany's greatest poet, author of Faust and The Sorrows of Young Werther; also a Weimar statesman, botanist and theorist of colour.
The 'Tiger of Mysore', a fierce opponent of the British East India Company who pioneered war rockets; killed defending his capital.

role.en: 4th US president, "Father of the Constitution" and the War of 1812

bio.en: The chief architect of the US Constitution and the Bill of Rights. His presidency saw the War of 1812 against Britain, during which British troops burned Washington and the White House in 1814.

role.en: priest who began Mexico's independence war

bio.en: Village priest whose 1810 'Cry of Dolores' launched the Mexican War of Independence; captured and executed by the Spanish.
Fulani scholar who led a jihad against the Hausa kings and founded the Sokoto Caliphate, West Africa's largest 19th-century state.

Aid to the American colonists emptied the treasury, and summoning the Estates General in 1789 opened the way to revolution. After the failed flight to Varennes he was deposed and executed in January 1793.

role.en: emperor who reformed the succession law, killed by conspirators

bio.en: Son of Catherine the Great. He introduced male-line succession and limited corvée labour to three days a week; his petty drill and unpredictability provoked a conspiracy, and he was murdered in the Mikhailovsky Castle.
Austrian-born wife of Louis XVI who became a symbol of royal extravagance and was guillotined during the French Revolution.

role.en: brother of Louis XVI who restored the Bourbons

bio.en: He spent more than twenty years in exile. Returning in 1814, he granted the Charter, a constitution; during Napoleon’s Hundred Days he fled to Ghent, returning after Waterloo.
Child prodigy and genius of Viennese Classicism who wrote over 600 works in 35 years, including The Marriage of Figaro, Don Giovanni and the Requiem.
Younger brother of Louis XVI and Louis XVIII, he hoped to restore the old order. His ordinances against press freedom sparked the July Revolution of 1830, and he died in exile.
United the Hawaiian Islands into a single kingdom by 1810 and kept them independent of the European powers.

role.en: 5th US president, the Monroe Doctrine and the "Era of Good Feelings"

bio.en: In 1823 he proclaimed the Monroe Doctrine, closing the Americas to further European colonization. Under him the US acquired Florida from Spain (1819) and adopted the Missouri Compromise (1820).
Author of A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), a founding text of feminism, and mother of Frankenstein author Mary Shelley.
Ukiyo-e master whose Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji includes The Great Wave off Kanagawa; a major influence on the Impressionists.
Tried to modernise the Ottoman Empire on European lines with his Nizam-i Cedid army; overthrown by the Janissaries and killed.

role.en: the Prince Regent who gave his name to the Regency era

bio.en: From 1811 to 1820 he ruled as Prince Regent for his ailing father, giving his name to the Regency era. He was known for extravagance, a scandalous marriage and a love of the arts, building the Royal Pavilion in Brighton and remodelling Buckingham Palace.
Developed Kant's ideas into a system that derives everything from the activity of the "I". His Addresses to the German Nation (1808) became a founding text of German nationalism.
Eora man who became a go-between for Aboriginal people and British settlers and visited England; the Opera House stands on Bennelong Point.

role.en: the 'Sailor King' under whom the Reform Act was passed

bio.en: A former naval officer known as the Sailor King. His reign saw the parliamentary Reform Act of 1832 and the abolition of slavery across most of the British Empire. He died without legitimate children, leaving the throne to his niece Victoria.

role.en: 6th US president, diplomat and opponent of slavery

bio.en: Son of John Adams and the first US minister to Russia. He won the presidency after the 1824 election was decided by the House; he then served 17 years in Congress, fighting slavery and defending the Amistad captives.

role.en: 7th US president, the Trail of Tears and the Jacksonian era

bio.en: Hero of the Battle of New Orleans (1815) and the first "people's president". He signed the Indian Removal Act (1830), which led to the Trail of Tears, and destroyed the Second Bank of the United States.
Tried to unite tribes from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico against American expansion; he died fighting alongside the British.

role.en: last Holy Roman Emperor, who dissolved the empire in 1806

bio.en: Defeated by Napoleon time and again, he proclaimed himself Emperor of Austria (as Francis I) in 1804 and laid down the Holy Roman crown in 1806. He married his daughter Marie Louise to Napoleon, and after Napoleon's fall hosted the Congress of Vienna with Metternich.
Revolutionary general turned emperor who conquered much of Europe and issued the Civil Code, before defeat in Russia in 1812 and at Waterloo.
Albanian officer who became pasha of Egypt, modernising its army, economy and schools and founding a dynasty that ruled until 1952.
Bridge between Classicism and Romanticism. Wrote nine symphonies and the Moonlight Sonata, composing the Ninth when completely deaf.

Saw history and thought as the development of Absolute Spirit through contradictions, dialectics, towards freedom and self-knowledge. Author of the Phenomenology of Spirit; both the Young Hegelians and Marxism grew from his work.
A Ngāpuhi chief who visited England and armed his people with muskets, sparking New Zealand's Musket Wars.

role.en: the "Citizen King", last king of France

bio.en: Of the Orléans branch of the Bourbons, he fought for the Revolution at Valmy as a young man. Brought to power by the July Revolution, he ruled in the interest of the bourgeoisie and was toppled by the revolution of 1848.

role.en: longest-serving shogun, for half a century

bio.en: Shogun 1787–1837. Early on, the regent Matsudaira Sadanobu carried out the Kansei Reforms; later the court sank into luxury, and Ienari fathered more than 50 children. In 1825 he ordered all foreign ships to be driven off by force.

Grandson of Catherine the Great, he began his reign with liberal reforms and created the ministries. He led Russia in the Patriotic War of 1812, entered Paris with the Allies and initiated the Holy Alliance.

role.en: liberator of Argentina, Chile and Peru

bio.en: Led his army across the Andes to free Chile and Peru from Spanish rule; national hero of Argentina.
Ruled Madagascar for 33 years, expelling missionaries and repelling French and British attempts to control the island.

role.en: sultan who overthrew the reformer Selim III

bio.en: He came to power in 1807 on a Janissary revolt against Selim III's reforms. As Alemdar Mustafa Pasha's troops marched on the palace in 1808 he ordered Selim killed; he was himself deposed and executed.
Led guerrilla forces against Spain in Upper Peru (Bolivia); a national heroine of both Bolivia and Argentina.

role.en: 8th US president, builder of the Democratic Party

bio.en: A New York politician who organized the Democratic Party and the first president born a US citizen. His term was overshadowed by the Panic of 1837 and a long depression.
'El Libertador' who led the independence of Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia, which is named after him.

role.en: 12th US president, general of the Mexican–American War

bio.en: A career soldier famed for his victory at Buena Vista (1847). He served only 16 months as president, dying in July 1850 amid the dispute over slavery in the new territories.

In 1826 he destroyed the Janissary corps and began building a European-style army, introducing the fez and ministries. Under him Greece won independence and Muhammad Ali of Egypt defeated the sultan's armies.
Gathered scattered clans into the Basotho nation on the fortress mountain of Thaba Bosiu and won a British protectorate that saved Lesotho from the Boers.
Revolutionised Zulu warfare with the short spear and 'bull horn' formation, building a powerful kingdom in southern Africa; killed by his brothers.

In The World as Will and Representation he argued that a blind, insatiable will underlies everything and life is suffering, relieved by art, compassion and renouncing desire. One of the first Western thinkers to draw on Indian philosophy.

role.en: 10th US president, first vice president to succeed on a death

bio.en: Took office in 1841 on the death of William Henry Harrison, setting the precedent of full succession. He secured the annexation of Texas (1845) and sided with the Confederacy in 1861.

role.en: 15th US president, on the eve of the Civil War

bio.en: The only US president who never married. He failed to stop the nation's breakup: by the end of his term seven Southern states had seceded and formed the Confederacy.

role.en: ailing emperor for whom Metternich governed, abdicated in 1848

bio.en: Epileptic son of Francis II, nicknamed "the Good". Metternich and a state council actually governed; after the revolution of 1848 he abdicated in favour of his nephew Franz Joseph and lived out his life in Prague Castle.

role.en: shogun who died just after the Black Ships arrived

bio.en: Shogun 1837–1853. Under him Mizuno Tadakuni pursued the failed Tenpō Reforms (1841–1843). In July 1853 Commodore Perry's squadron entered Edo Bay, and Ieyoshi died a few days later.

His Philosophical Letters reflected on Russia's place between West and East and its separation from European history. After the first letter appeared in 1836 he was officially declared insane; the debate split Westernizers and Slavophiles.

role.en: 11th US president, the Mexican–American War and the push to the Pacific

bio.en: In a single term he extended the US to the Pacific: the Oregon Treaty with Britain (1846) and the Mexican–American War (1846–1848), which brought California and New Mexico into the Union.

role.en: emperor who crushed the Decembrist revolt

bio.en: He began his reign by crushing the Decembrist revolt. He strengthened autocracy and bureaucracy; his reign produced the Digest of Laws and the first railway, and he died amid the losing Crimean War.

role.en: French philosopher, founder of positivism and sociology

bio.en: Taught that knowledge passes through three stages, theological, metaphysical and scientific, and that only what experience confirms is reliable: the founding idea of positivism. He also coined the word 'sociology' for the science of society.
Founder of modern Russian literature, author of Eugene Onegin and The Bronze Horseman. Killed in a duel at 37.

role.en: 13th US president, the Compromise of 1850 and the Perry Expedition

bio.en: Became president on Taylor's death and signed the Compromise of 1850, including the harsh Fugitive Slave Act. He sent Commodore Perry's squadron that opened Japan to the outside world.
Leading figure of French Romanticism, author of The Hunchback of Notre-Dame and Les Misérables.
Leader of the Transcendentalists. In Nature (1836) and Self-Reliance he urged people to seek truth in their own souls and in nature rather than in authority and tradition.
He signed the Kansas–Nebraska Act (1854), which left slavery to settlers' vote and led to "Bleeding Kansas". He bought southern Arizona and New Mexico from Mexico (the Gadsden Purchase, 1853).

A Young Hegelian and author of The Ego and Its Own (1844), which rejected the state, morality and any idea set above the individual. He is seen as a forerunner of individualist anarchism and existentialism.
A Zapotec orphan who became president of Mexico, separated church and state and defeated the French-backed Emperor Maximilian.
Developed Bentham's utilitarianism and wrote On Liberty (1859): power may be used against an individual only to prevent harm to others. One of the first MPs to call for votes for women.

role.en: last French monarch, who surrendered to Prussia at Sedan

bio.en: Nephew of Napoleon I, elected president in 1848, he made himself emperor after the coup of 1851. Baron Haussmann rebuilt Paris under him; in 1870 he surrendered at Sedan.

role.en: 17th US president, the first impeachment and the Alaska Purchase

bio.en: He succeeded the assassinated Lincoln and clashed with Congress over Reconstruction. In 1868 he became the first president impeached, acquitted by the Senate by a single vote; Alaska was bought from Russia under him (1867).
Sailed around the world on HMS Beagle; in On the Origin of Species (1859) he set out evolution by natural selection.
President during the American Civil War who issued the Emancipation Proclamation; assassinated in 1865.
Polish Romantic composer living in Paris, known for his nocturnes, mazurkas, polonaises and two piano concertos.
Author of Oliver Twist, David Copperfield, Great Expectations and A Christmas Carol.
Survived the near-destruction of her people during Tasmania's colonisation; long called the 'last Tasmanian', she became a symbol of Aboriginal tragedy.
Opera reformer, composer of The Ring of the Nibelung and Tristan und Isolde, and founder of the Bayreuth Festival.
Scottish missionary who crossed Africa coast to coast and was the first European to see Victoria Falls.

Put the individual at the centre of philosophy: personal choice, anxiety, and faith as a "leap" rather than a conclusion of reasoning. Seen as the forerunner of existentialism; he published many books under pseudonyms.

role.en: first Chancellor of the German Empire

bio.en: Prussian minister-president who unified Germany in 1871 and became the German Empire's first chancellor.
Byron's daughter who described Babbage's Analytical Engine and wrote what is regarded as the first computer program.

role.en: Premier of New South Wales, 'Father of Federation'

bio.en: Five times premier of New South Wales; his 1889 Tenterfield speech launched the drive to federate the colonies into Australia.
Emperor who abolished serfdom in 1861 and carried out judicial, local-government and military reforms; assassinated in 1881.
Author of Capital and, with Engels, The Communist Manifesto; his ideas became the foundation of Marxism.
Escaped from slavery to become a leading orator, writer and figure of the American abolitionist movement.
Reigned for 63 years (1837–1901), the height of the British Empire, an age that bears her name.
Famed for nursing the wounded in the Crimean War; founder of modern nursing and a pioneer of medical statistics.

A manufacturer's son who described workers' lives in The Condition of the Working Class in England. He co-wrote The Communist Manifesto with Marx and edited the second and third volumes of Capital after Marx's death.
Author of Crime and Punishment, The Idiot and The Brothers Karamazov, novels of deep psychological and moral inquiry.
A founder of microbiology who developed pasteurization and vaccines against anthrax and rabies.
Escaped slavery and returned south many times to guide dozens of people to freedom on the Underground Railroad.

role.en: 18th US president, commanding general of the Union Army

bio.en: The general who accepted Lee's surrender in 1865. As president he defended the rights of freed Black Americans and fought the Ku Klux Klan, but his administration was shaken by corruption scandals.

role.en: 19th US president, the end of Reconstruction

bio.en: He won the disputed 1876 election through the Compromise of 1877, under which federal troops left the South, ending Reconstruction.
The Edict of Gülhane (1839) opened the Tanzimat era, proclaiming equality of subjects before the law. He fought Russia in the Crimean War alongside Britain and France and built Dolmabahçe Palace.

role.en: shogun under whom Japan opened its ports to the West

bio.en: A sickly shogun, 1853–1858. His rule saw the Convention of Kanagawa with the United States (1854), which opened Shimoda and Hakodate, and the Harris Treaty of commerce (1858); the dispute over his heir split the elite.
Brazil's last emperor, reigning for nearly 50 years (1831–1889); slavery was abolished in Brazil during his reign.
Author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina, one of the greatest novelists in world literature and a moral and religious thinker.
Fought the French for more than 15 years with an army that had its own arms workshops; one of West Africa's most determined resisters of colonisation.
Became president after James Garfield's assassination in 1881. He signed the Pendleton Act (1883), replacing the spoils system with merit-based hiring of officials.

role.en: Russian philosopher, founder of Russian cosmism

bio.en: A librarian at the Rumyantsev Museum in Moscow whom Tolstoy and Dostoevsky admired as a thinker. In The Philosophy of the Common Task he called on humanity to unite, overcome death and settle space; he guided the young Tsiolkovsky's reading at the library.
American poet who published little in her lifetime; her nearly 1,800 poems, printed posthumously, reshaped American verse.

role.en: emperor of Austria-Hungary for 68 years, who took it into the First World War

bio.en: He took the throne at eighteen in 1848, lost the wars of 1859 and 1866 and by the Compromise of 1867 turned his empire into Austria-Hungary. He outlived the suicide of his son Rudolf and the murder of his wife Elisabeth ("Sisi"), and in 1914 declared war on Serbia.

role.en: first sultan to visit Western Europe

bio.en: In 1867 he visited Paris and London and built an ironclad navy, but foreign loans ruined the treasury and the state defaulted in 1875. Deposed in 1876, he was found dead days later.
The Lakota holy man who united the tribes that wiped out Custer's force at the Little Bighorn in 1876.

role.en: 23rd US president, the Sherman Antitrust Act

bio.en: Grandson of President William Henry Harrison. He signed the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890), and six new states, from North Dakota to Wyoming, joined the Union under him.

role.en: chemist, creator of the periodic table

bio.en: Formulated the periodic law of chemical elements (1869) and predicted the properties of elements not yet discovered.
American writer and humorist, author of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn.
Effectively ruled Qing China for nearly half a century, from 1861 until her death, as regent for young emperors.
Kazakh scholar and Russian army officer who reached Kashgar in 1858–1859 and was among the first to describe East Turkestan.

role.en: last shogun, who handed power back to the emperor

bio.en: He became shogun in early 1867 and returned power to the emperor that November. After losing the Battle of Toba–Fushimi in 1868 he surrendered Edo without a fight and lived 45 more years as a private man, taking up photography.

role.en: 22nd and 24th US president, two non-consecutive terms

bio.en: The first president to serve two non-consecutive terms (1885–1889 and 1893–1897). He fought congressional spending with a record number of vetoes; his second term faced the Panic of 1893 and the Pullman Strike.
The last monarch of the Hawaiian Kingdom, overthrown in 1893; composer of the song 'Aloha ʻOe'.
Russian explorer who led expeditions to the Ussuri region, Mongolia, China and Tibet; described the wild horse named after him.
Founder of pragmatism: the meaning of an idea lies in its practical consequences. He worked for thirty years for the US Coast Survey and laid the foundations of semiotics, the study of signs.
Composer of the ballets Swan Lake, The Sleeping Beauty and The Nutcracker, the opera Eugene Onegin and six symphonies.
His Impression, Sunrise gave Impressionism its name; painted the Haystacks, Rouen Cathedral and Water Lilies series.

role.en: Queen Mother of Ejisu, war leader

bio.en: Led the Ashanti uprising of 1900 after the British governor demanded the sacred Golden Stool.

role.en: king of the Edwardian era who helped forge the Entente Cordiale

bio.en: Queen Victoria's eldest son, who waited almost 60 years for the throne. He gave his name to the Edwardian era; related to many of Europe's monarchs, he helped bring about the rapprochement with France known as the Entente Cordiale of 1904.

role.en: the 'Red Sultan' who dissolved the first parliament

bio.en: He granted the 1876 constitution but dissolved parliament in 1878 and ruled autocratically for 30 years through pan-Islamism and a secret police, building the Hejaz Railway. The Armenian massacres of 1894–1896 earned him the name 'Red Sultan'; the Young Turks deposed him in 1909.
A Harvard professor, author of The Principles of Psychology (1890) and of the phrase "stream of consciousness". He made pragmatism famous: true ideas are those that prove themselves in experience.

role.en: 25th US president, the Spanish–American War and overseas empire

bio.en: Under him the US won the war with Spain (1898), gaining the Philippines, Puerto Rico and Guam, and annexed Hawaii. He was assassinated by an anarchist in Buffalo in 1901.
Emperor who founded Addis Ababa and defeated Italy at Adwa (1896), preserving Ethiopian independence.

role.en: sultan under whom the empire entered World War I

bio.en: A constitutional monarch with no real power, as the Young Turks ran the country. In 1914 the empire entered World War I on Germany's side in his name and a jihad was proclaimed against the Entente.

Proclaimed the "death of God" and called for a revaluation of all values, introducing the Übermensch, the will to power and eternal recurrence. A professor at Basel at 24, he spent his last 11 years mentally incapacitated.

He took the throne after his father's assassination by revolutionaries and rolled back liberal reforms. Russia fought no wars during his reign, which saw construction of the Trans-Siberian Railway begin and an alliance with France.

role.en: shogun who wed the emperor's sister to bind court and shogunate

bio.en: He became shogun in 1858 at 12. To unite court and shogunate he married Princess Kazu, sister of Emperor Kōmei, and in 1863 became the first shogun in 229 years to visit Kyoto; he died in Osaka during the second Chōshū expedition.
Inventor of the phonograph, a practical incandescent lamp and early power grids; held over a thousand patents.
Scottish-born inventor who patented the telephone in the US in 1876 and worked as a teacher of the deaf.
Led the campaign that made New Zealand, in 1893, the first country to give women the vote.

The creator of modern logic: his Begriffsschrift (1879) introduced a formal language in which reasoning can be checked like a calculation. His work on sense and reference became a cornerstone of analytic philosophy.
Studied the physiology of digestion and discovered conditioned reflexes; the first Russian Nobel laureate (1904).
